title: Celsus’s darkness and the light that heals the blind
source_text: Τοῦτο δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς προκειμένοις ὁ Κέλσος εἶπεν ἀληθὲς. ὅτι ἀκούσας τις αὐτοῦ τῶν λόγων ἀποκρίνεται, ἰδὼν δ᾿ ὅτι λόγοι σκότους εἰσὶν οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ, ὅτι σκότος μου τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν προβάλλεις. Κέλσος μὲν ουν καὶ οἱ παραπλήσιοι αὐτῷ προβάλλειν σκότον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἡμῶν θέλουσιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ τῷ φωτὶ τοῦ λόγου ἐξαφανίζομεν τὸ σκότος τῶν ἀσεβῶν δογμάτων. εἴποι δ᾿ ἂν ὁ Χριστιανὸς πρὸς Κέλσον οὐδὲν ἐναργὲς καὶ πληκτικὸν λέγοντα τό· οὐδὲν ἐναργὲς βλέπω ἐν τοῖς σοῖς λόγοις. οὐκ ἐκ σκότου τοίνυν εἰς λαμπρὸν φῶς προάγει ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος, ἀλλὰ βούλεται ἐκ φωτὸς μεταστῆσαι εἰς σκότον, τιθεὶς „τὸ σκότος“ εἶναι „φῶς καὶ τὸ φῶς σκότος“ καὶ ὑποκείμενος τῷ καλῶς εἰρημένῳ ὑπὸ Ἡσαΐου τὸν τρόπον τοῦτον· „οὐαὶ οἱ τιθέντες τὸ σκότος φῶς καὶ τὸ φῶς σκότος.“ ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς. ἀνοίξαντος τοῦ λόγου τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῶν, ὁρῶντες διαφορὰν φωτὸς καὶ σκότους ἐν φωτὶ μὲν παντὶ τρόπῳ ἵστασθαι προαιρούμεθα, τῷ δὲ σκότῳ οὐδαμῶς προσεῖναι βουλόμεθα. ἔμψυχον δὲ τυγχάνον τὸ ἀληθινὸν φῶς ἐπίσταται, τίνι μὲν δεικτέον ἔσται τὰς μαρμαρυγὰς τίνι δὲ φῶς, οὐ παριστάντος αὐτοῦ τὴν λαμπρότητα ἑαυτοῦ διὰ τὴν ἔτι δὲ φῶς, οὐ ἀσθένειαν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐκείνου. εἰ δ᾿ ὅλως χρὴ λέγειν κολάζεσθαι καὶ βλάπτεσθαι ὄψιν. τίνος ἂν ἄλλου φήσωμεν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ταῦτα πάσχειν ἢ τοῦ ὑπὸ τῆς περὶ θεοῦ ἀγνοίας συνεχομένου καὶ τοῦ ὑπὸ τῶν παθῶν ἐμποδιζομένου βλέπειν ἀλήθειαν; Χριστιανοὶ μὲν οὖν οὐδαμῶς νομίζουσι πηροῦσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν Κέλσου ἤ τινος ἀλλοτρίου θεοσεβείας λόγων· οἱ δ᾿ αἰσθανόμενοι ἑαυτῶν πηρουμένων ὑπὸ τοῦ κατακολουθεῖν ὄχλοις πλανωμένων καὶ ἔθνεσιν ἑορταζόντων δαιμονίοις προσίτωσαν τῷ χαριζομένῳ ὀφθαλμοὺς λόγῳ, ἵν᾿ ὁμοίως τοῖς παρὰ τῇ ὁδῷ ἐῤῥιμμένοις πτωχοῖς καὶ τυφλοῖς. ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ θεραπευθεῖσι διὰ τὸ εἰρηκέναι αὐτῷ· „υἱὲ Δαυΐδ, ἐλέησόν με,“ ἐλεηθέντες ἀπολάβωσι τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς καινοὺς καὶ καλοὺς, ὁποίους λόγος θεοῦ δημιουργήσαι ἄν.
pass_a_gloss: This Celsus said true (ἀληθής) in the things set forth (πρόκειμαι): that someone having heard his words (λόγοι) answers, having seen that his words are words of darkness (σκότος), 'that you put darkness before (προβάλλω) my eyes.' Celsus then and those like (παραπλήσιος) him wish to put darkness before our eyes, but we by the light of the Word make vanish (ἐξαφανίζω) the darkness of impious doctrines (ἀσεβῆ δόγματα). The Christian would say to Celsus, saying nothing clear (ἐναργής) and striking (πληκτικός): 'I see nothing clear in your words.' Not out of darkness then into bright light does Celsus lead us, but wishes to remove (μεθίστημι) [us] from light into darkness, putting (τίθημι) darkness [to be] light and light darkness, and being subject (ὑπόκειμαι) to what was well said by Isaiah in this manner: 'Woe (οὐαί) to those putting darkness light and light darkness.' But we, the Word having opened (ἀνοίγω) the eyes of our soul, seeing the difference of light and darkness, choose (προαιρέομαι) in every way to stand in light, and in no way wish to be near (πρόσειμι) the darkness. Being living (ἔμψυχος), the true (ἀληθινός) light knows (ἐπίσταμαι) to whom the gleams (μαρμαρυγαί) must be shown and to whom light, not presenting its own brightness (λαμπρότης) because of the still [present] weakness (ἀσθένεια) in that one's eyes. If at all one must speak of sight afflicted (κολάζω) and harmed (βλάπτω), whose eyes would we say suffer this other than of the one held (συνέχω) by ignorance (ἄγνοια) about God and hindered (ἐμποδίζω) by passions (πάθη) from seeing truth? Christians then in no way think they are blinded (πηρόω) by the words of Celsus or of anyone alien (ἀλλότριος) to piety (θεοσέβεια); but those perceiving themselves being blinded by following (κατακολουθέω) crowds (ὄχλοι) going astray (πλανάω) and nations celebrating festivals (ἑορτάζω) to demons (δαιμόνια), let them approach (πρόσειμι) the Word that grants (χαρίζομαι) eyes, so that, like the poor (πτωχός) and blind (τυφλός) cast (ῥίπτω) by the road (ὁδός), healed (θεραπεύω) by Jesus because of having said to him 'Son of David, have mercy (ἐλεέω) on me', having received mercy they may receive back (ἀπολαμβάνω) the eyes new (καινός) and beautiful (καλός), such as the Word of God would craft (δημιουργέω).
pass_b_english: This, however, Celsus said truly in the passage before us: that someone who has heard his words, and has seen that they are words of darkness, answers, “You cast darkness before my eyes.” Celsus, then, and those like him wish to cast darkness before our eyes; but we, by the light of the Word, make the darkness of impious doctrines vanish. And the Christian might well say to Celsus, who says nothing clear or compelling, “I see nothing clearly in your words.” So Celsus does not lead us out of darkness into bright light. Rather, he wishes to move us from light into darkness, making “darkness light and light darkness”, and he falls under what Isaiah rightly said in these words: “Woe to those who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isaiah 5:20).

But we, since the Word has opened the eyes of our soul and we see the difference between light and darkness, choose in every way to stand in the light, and have no wish at all to come near the darkness. The true light (John 1:9), being alive, knows to whom its full brilliance should be shown and to whom only light; and, because of the weakness still in a man’s eyes, it does not display its own brightness to him.

And if we must speak at all of sight being afflicted and harmed, whose eyes would we say suffer this, if not the eyes of one held fast by ignorance about God and kept by the passions from seeing the truth? Christians, then, by no means think they are blinded by the words of Celsus, or of anyone else who is a stranger to the worship of God. But let those who perceive that they are being blinded by following crowds that go astray, and nations that hold festivals to demons, come to the Word who grants eyes, so that, like the poor and blind men lying beside the road who were healed by Jesus because they had said to him, “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark 10:46–48; Luke 18:35–39), they too may receive mercy and get back their eyes, new and beautiful, such as the Word of God would create.

choices.choice: Quoted words of Celsus’s imagined speaker: ‘You cast darkness before my eyes’; ‘I see nothing clear’ is Celsus’s phrase turned back on him by the Christian. Doubtful reading: the staged text has a dittography, τίνι δὲ φῶς, οὐ παριστάντος αὐτοῦ τὴν λαμπρότητα ἑαυτοῦ διὰ τὴν ἔτι δὲ φῶς, οὐ ἀσθένειαν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐκείνου; translated as if it read διὰ τὴν ἔτι ἀσθένειαν, with the repeated ‘δὲ φῶς, οὐ’ set aside as a copying error; check against the Perseus TEI. Also the stray full stops after ἀλλ’ ἡμεῖς, after ὄψιν, and after τυφλοῖς in the staged text are treated as punctuation slips, not sentence breaks. ‘Its full brilliance’ renders τὰς μαρμαρυγάς (the dazzling gleams, as opposed to plain light). Isaiah 5:20 LXX οὐαὶ οἱ λέγοντες ... τιθέντες τὸ σκότος φῶς καὶ τὸ φῶς σκότος; Origen’s wording matches the second clause. ‘The true light’ is a clear allusion to John 1:9. ‘Son of David, have mercy on me’ (singular): Mark 10:48 and Luke 18:39 give exactly υἱὲ Δαυίδ, ἐλέησόν με (Mark 10:47 and Luke 18:38 add ‘Jesus’), so the citation runs to those verses (Bartimaeus, sitting by the road, a beggar); Origen’s plural ‘poor and blind men’ may also take in Matthew 20:30 (two blind men by the road, ‘have mercy on us’), recorded in bible_refs but not cited inline. ‘Opened the eyes of our soul’ may echo Ephesians 1:18 or Luke 24:31; uncertain, not cited.
reordered the first sentence so 'answers' follows both participles ('who has heard his words, and has seen that they are words of darkness, answers')
'I see nothing clear in your words' -> 'I see nothing clearly in your words' (same English as Celsus's phrase in chapter 66, which Origen turns back on him)
'choose by every means ... want nothing whatever to do with the darkness' -> 'choose in every way ... have no wish at all to come near the darkness' (παντὶ τρόπῳ; προσεῖναι = come near)
last clause of the true-light sentence now keeps the causal 'because of the weakness still in a man's eyes' (διὰ τὴν ἔτι ἀσθένειαν), which the old wording had folded away
'Then, like the poor ... they too may' -> 'so that, like the poor ... they too may' (ἵνα purpose clause)
citation widened to Mark 10:46–48; Luke 18:35–39: the exact cry 'Son of David, have mercy on me' without 'Jesus' is Mark 10:48 and Luke 18:39; bible_refs updated
